verses.125:2a: Então {replere} de {gaudium} a nossa boca: * e a nossa língua de {ex2}.
verses.125:4: Fazei voltar, Senhor, {cap4}, * como uma torrente {auster}.
verses.125:6b: Vindo, porém, virão {ex6}, * {portantes} os seus feixes.

decisions.why: The Latin is a gerund with its own subject in the nominative (ἐν τῷ ἐπιστρέψαι κύριον, the Greek articular infinitive): 'in the Lord's turning'. It has no tense; the perfect *facti sumus* of the second colon puts it in the past. Ps 9:4 met the same build (*In converténdo inimícum meum retrórsum*) and rendered it *Ao fazer voltar para trás o meu inimigo*; there the subject was the speaker's and needed no naming.

options.label: Quando o Senhor fez voltar
options.note: Draft. A temporal clause, the way Portuguese says 'in the doing of X by Y'; the tense is taken from *facti sumus*. DRB 'When the lord brought back', MS1932 'Quando o Senhor fez voltar' — both Vulgate witnesses build it so.

options.label: Ao fazer o Senhor voltar
options.note: Keeps the infinitive, as 9:4 did. With a named subject between the two verbs it is bookish and splits *fazer voltar*; refused.

decisions.why: The glossary row *captívitas → cativeiro* names 125:1 and 125:4 and gives the build for 125:4 in advance (*Fazei voltar, Senhor, o nosso cativeiro*), after 52:7 *quando Deus fizer voltar o cativeiro do seu povo*. The abstract noun stands for the captives (a Hebraism the Greek and Latin keep: αἰχμαλωσίαν). MS1932 and the CNBB Liturgia das Horas (consult/web-lh-salmo-125-126.md, from the Hebrew) say 'os cativos'.

options.label: o cativeiro
options.note: Draft, by the glossary and 52:7. The Latin's noun; 'make the captivity turn back' is the Latin's own figure, and the same verb and object repeat across 125:1 and 125:4 as in the Latin.

options.label: os cativos
options.note: MS1932. Plainer, but explains the figure (a person for an abstract) and breaks the glossary row that 13:7, 52:7 and 84:2 follow.

decisions.latin: facti sumus sicut consoláti … facti sumus lætántes
decisions.why: The psalm says *facti sumus* twice, at the end of its two halves of thanksgiving, so one verb twice. The glossary row *fíeri* gives *tornar-se* for a state that comes upon the subject (13:3a, 82:11, 118:83), and 78:4 *facti sumus oppróbrium* → *Tornamo-nos uma afronta* is the same form. The Tuesday Vespers antiphon is 125:3 whole (*Magnificávit Dóminus * fácere nobíscum: facti sumus lætántes*, Psalmi major, Day2 Vespera), so the colon must read alone.

options.label: tornamo-nos
options.note: Draft, by the fíeri row and 78:4. A change of state, as the Latin says.

options.label: ficamos
options.note: The plainest Brazilian verb for 'became (a state)'; precedent 50:9 *dealbári → ficar mais branco*. One syllable shorter. Kept as the option in case the reflexive sounds stiff at a cadence start.

decisions.why: The Latin follows the Greek ὡς παρακεκλημένοι, 'as men comforted', against the Hebrew 'like dreamers' (which the Diurnal and the CNBB have: *parecia um sonho*, *parecíamos sonhar*). The Latin's sense is kept.

options.label: como consolados
options.note: Draft. DRB 'like men comforted'. The participle as the Latin has it.

options.label: como quem é consolado
options.note: Clearer for the ear that *consolados* is a condition, not a verb; two syllables longer.

options.label: cheios de consolação
options.note: MS1932. Drops *sicut* (the Latin says 'as if', not 'full of'); refused.

decisions.why: The glossary row *gáudium → júbilo* (open, for a ruling) names 125:2a; it is applied at 20:7, 29:12, 50:10. *Alegria* is lætítia's; *gozo* is heard sexually in Brazil (the row's note). The passive *replétum est* is given as the Portuguese se-passive (grammar, D2).

options.label: se encheu de júbilo
options.note: Draft, by the row. The CNBB (from the Hebrew) also says *encheu-se … nossa boca*.

options.label: foi cheia de júbilo
options.note: The Latin's passive as a passive, as the open *replére (passive)* row does at 64:5b, 64:12. Stiffer.

options.label: se encheu de alegria
options.note: The familiar word; takes lætítia's, and *alegres* in 125:3 renders another Latin root (lætántes).

decisions.latin: exsultatióne … in exsultatióne metent … cum exsultatióne
decisions.why: The Latin has *exsultátio* three times (ἀγαλλίασις each time) and the psalm's two halves close on it; the glossary row *exsultátio → exultação* is working, kept in 41:5b, 99:2b, 104:43, 117:15 although blind readers have repeatedly listed it as unfamiliar. *In* of manner (125:5) and *cum* (125:6b) both give *com*, as 99:2b.

options.label: exultação
options.note: Draft, by the row; the Latin's repetition kept across the three places.

options.label: alegria
options.note: MS1932 at 125:5 and the CNBB (*ceifarão com alegria*) — the line as Brazilians know it. Takes lætítia's word; refused under the glossary.

decisions.latin: Magnificávit Dóminus fácere cum eis … Magnificávit Dóminus fácere nobíscum
decisions.why: The Latin follows the Greek ἐμεγάλυνεν κύριος τοῦ ποιῆσαι, 'the Lord made great the doing': a verb of making-great governing an infinitive. Portuguese cannot say it verb for verb (*engrandeceu o fazer* is not a sentence). Every witness turns it into 'did great things' (DRB, MS1932). The two lines repeat the phrase (the end of 2b is the head of 3), so one wording twice; 125:3 opens the Tuesday Vespers antiphon. The glossary's *magnália → as grandes coisas* (70:19, 105:21) is another Latin word; the two never meet.

options.label: Grandes coisas fez o Senhor
options.note: Draft. MS1932's order: the greatness comes first, as *Magnificávit* does, and the phrase is a familiar liturgical build.

options.label: O Senhor fez grandes coisas
options.note: Plain order. Loses the Latin's fronted verb of greatness.

options.label: Maravilhas fez o Senhor
options.note: The CNBB's word (from the Hebrew). *Maravilhas* is mirabília's; refused.

decisions.why: The Latin and Greek say 'with' (μετ᾿ αὐτῶν). DRB and MS1932 turn it to 'for'. The CNBB Liturgia das Horas, prayed daily in Brazil, keeps 'with': *Maravilhas fez com eles o Senhor … fez conosco o Senhor* (verified, consult/web-lh-salmo-125-126.md) — so *fazer com* is a line Brazilian ears already know in this psalm.

options.label: com eles / conosco
options.note: Draft. The Latin's preposition; 'did great things with us' = dealt greatly with us.

options.label: por eles / por nós
options.note: DRB 'for them', MS1932 'em favor deles … por nós'. Explains the relation; kept as option.

decisions.why: *Auster* is first the south wind and by metonymy the south (Lewis & Short, both senses); Greek νότος is the same pair. DRB 'as a stream in the south' and MS1932 'na terra do meio-dia' read the region; Augustine reads the wind — the warm south wind melts the ice and fills the winter torrents (Enarr. in Ps. 125, checked in consult/newadvent-augustine-ps125.htm). No plain Portuguese word keeps both: *austro* has both senses in the dictionary but is unknown to most ears; *sul* is the region, *vento sul* the wind (the glossary gives *Auster → o vento sul* at 77:26, where the wind is plain from the verb).

options.label: no sul
options.note: Draft. Both Vulgate-family witnesses; the image of the torrent that fills the dry south is plain. Loses Augustine's wind.

options.label: no vento sul
options.note: Augustine's reading and L&S's first sense; the glossary's word at 77:26. Closes the ambiguity the other way, and a torrent 'in the south wind' needs Augustine to be understood.

options.label: no austro
options.note: Keeps both senses, as the Latin does, but would need a footnote (rule 5); refused.

decisions.why: The Latin sets the joy first and ends on the verb, against *in lácrimis* at the end of the first colon (a chiasm: sow — tears / joy — reap). *Metere* is to reap, to cut the grain; *ceifar* is the exact image and goes with the sheaves of 125:6b. The CNBB has *ceifarão com alegria* (verified), MS1932 *com alegria ceifarão*, so *ceifar* is the word Brazilian ears know here.

options.label: com exultação ceifarão
options.note: Draft. The Latin's order and chiasm, and MS1932's; ends on the verb, an oxytone, as the Latin ends on *metent*.

options.label: ceifarão com exultação
options.note: Plain order (the CNBB's). Loses the chiasm; the verse would end on the same word as 125:2a and 125:6b's mediant.

options.label: com exultação colherão
options.note: *Colher* is the commoner harvest verb but is 'gather'; *ceifar* keeps the sickle and goes with *feixes*.

decisions.why: The Latin keeps the Greek's doubled verb (πορευόμενοι ἐπορεύοντο, the Hebrew infinitive absolute) and sets *Veniéntes … vénient* against it in 125:6b: going went / coming will come. The repetition and the pairing are the Latin's (rule 2); DRB 'Going they went and wept'. The colon is also sung alone as an antiphon of the Common of Apostles (*Eúntes ibant * et flebant, mitténtes sémina sua*, Commune/C1).

options.label: Indo, iam e choravam
options.note: Draft. Both forms of *ire* in the Latin's order, and the same build as 125:6b *Vindo, porém, virão*, so the pairing is heard.

options.label: Iam indo e choravam
options.note: The Brazilian progressive *ir + gerúndio* ('they kept on going'); natural, keeps both forms, but the order no longer mirrors 125:6b.

options.label: Iam e vinham chorando
options.note: MS1932. Adds a coming the Latin puts only in 125:6b and drops the doubling; refused.

decisions.why: *Portáre* is to carry; *manípulus* is a handful, a bundle (L&S) — the reaper's sheaf. MS1932 *trazendo os seus feixes*; the CNBB *carregando os seus feixes* (verified).

options.label: trazendo
options.note: Draft. MS1932. Goes with *Vindo … virão*: they come bringing.

options.label: carregando
options.note: The CNBB's; the weight is heard, one syllable longer.

choices.125:1: No title line (*Canticum graduum*): D7, as in ps120 and ps133. The Latin's colon ends with ':' and so does the Portuguese.
choices.125:2b: *dicent* is future in the Latin and the Greek (ἐροῦσιν) — 'then they will say among the nations' — after the past of 125:1–2a; kept (DRB 'Then shall they say'). The CNBB (from the Hebrew) has *se dizia*. *gentes → nações* (glossary). The quoted words are not set in quotation marks, as the Latin has none; the capital after the colon marks them.
choices.125:3: The whole verse is the Tuesday Vespers antiphon (Psalmi major, Day2 Vespera) and reads alone.
choices.125:4: *Convérte* → *Fazei voltar*: the causative the captívitas row prescribes for 125:4; *fazei* is not a homograph of a first-person past (*fiz*). *torrens → torrente* (glossary; 7 lines), singular as the Latin, with an indefinite article as a simile needs.
choices.125:5: *lágrimas* before the mark is a proparoxytone; the Latin *lácrimis* is one too, at the same place.
choices.125:6a: *mitténtes sémina sua* → *lançando as suas sementes*: the sower's cast (MS1932 *lançavam*). *semen* → *sementes* here, not *descendência*: D32's exception, the verse itself is a sowing.
choices.125:6b: *autem* → *porém*, after the participle, where the Latin has it. *manípulos → feixes* (MS1932, CNBB).

audit.note: Psalm-level draft from consult/parallels/ps125.md, the glossary rows captívitas, convértere, fíeri, gáudium, exsultátio, torrens, semen (D32), and a fetched CNBB Liturgia das Horas text (consult/web-lh-salmo-125-126.md) to check what circulates in Brazil: it confirms *ceifarão*, *feixes* and *fazer com / conosco*. Augustine on *Auster* checked in consult/newadvent-augustine-ps125.htm. Liturgical uses found by grep in the DO Latin: 125:3 is the Tuesday Vespers antiphon; 125:6a the antiphon *Eúntes ibant* of the Common of Apostles (C1); 125:5–6 the Tract of the martyrs (C3, C3a; Mass 01-19, 01-20, 08-08 …), whose text reads *in gáudio metent* where the psalm has *in exsultatióne* — the psalm's word is followed. Hard readings: *magnificávit … fácere*, *in Austro*, *eúntes ibant*.

Hard checks pass (ids and marks). Soft flags accepted: 125:2a first colon +3 (the counter does not elide *se‿encheu*, *júbilo‿a*; about +1 when said); 125:2b and 125:3 second/first colon −3 (the Latin's infinitive *fácere* is folded into *fez*, see decision `magnif`); 125:6b first colon −5 (the Latin's long participle and verb, *Veniéntes … vénient … exsultatióne*, against short Portuguese *Vindo … virão*; nothing to add that the Latin has). 125:5 mediant *lágrimas* is proparoxytone, as *lácrimis* is.
